title: A starry superbubble
caption: The emission nebula Sh 2-305, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A gently glowing patch of sky fills this image. It is in fact Sh 2-305, a hot bubble of hydrogen gas lit up by intense radiation from nearby stars. Clouds like this are called emission nebulae, or HII regions, pronounced H-two.

The ultraviolet light behind the glow is thought to come from at least two O-type stars, and probably several others. O-type stars are the brightest and hottest kind known. They can hold up to 90 times the Sun's mass and shine one million times as brightly. Their radiation strips electrons from the hydrogen, which then glows.

Sh 2-305 is part of something much bigger. With five neighboring bubbles, it belongs to a giant complex of dense dust and gas clouds, and on a larger scale to an enormous ring called the GS234-02 star-forming supershell. The supershell sits in the Milky Way's Perseus arm, toward the constellation Puppis.

understand.summary: The VLT's FORS2 instrument took this visible-light image through B, V, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
filters: 440 nm · Optical B (Very Large Telescope FORS2)

understand.eye: The glow is faint, and the hydrogen filter and long exposures make it far more visible than it would be to the eye.

explore: The picture was taken through the ESO Cosmic Gems program, which turns telescope time unsuitable for science into outreach images, using the FORS instrument on the Very Large Telescope. The data also go into ESO's science archive for astronomers.
alt: A gently glowing bubble of hydrogen gas scattered with stars.
